began the lesson focusing on main idea and key details. However, after monitoring student understanding, it became clear that the scholars were not yet secure with identifying the main idea. I adjusted the lesson in the moment and narrowed the focus to main idea only.

To support their understanding, I introduced a visual scaffold using three labeled boxes: Too Small, Too Big, and Just Right. This helped students distinguish between a single detail (too small), the general topic (too big), and a complete main idea that includes all key examples (just right).

This adjustment allowed both scholars to correctly identify the main idea by the end of the lesson.

I kind of improvised a game because as we were leaving the class the class started playing a game and Sadie really wanted to play the game so I adapted our lesson into a place value game. So as an example on the ground I put down H,T,O for hundreds, tens, and ones. Then I wrote the number 362 on my board. Then I had activity index cards such as 'clap your hands, jump like a frog, shoulder shrugs, etc.' So I put a card on each H,T,O paper. So they realized on the H they had to do clap their hands 3 times because there are 3 hundreds in 362. For the tens they had to jump 6 times because there are 6 tens in 362. And do 2 shoulder shrugs because there are 2 ones in 362. Was a fun kinesthetic activity we kind of improvised.

When we returned, the class teacher continued reviewing material for the upcoming exam, and we worked on the problem alongside the class. After the review, the class teacher directed scholars to another activity. During this transition, another scholar (whose shadow was at lunch) came into our area and knocked A’Lore’s knit ear warmer/headband onto the floor. I calmly asked the scholar to return and pick it up; after some prompting, he did so but knocked it over again. The class teacher addressed the behavior. A’Lore was then given a choice to continue her review packet or begin the math lesson. She initially chose the packet but became frustrated with the next problem and was no longer receptive to redirection. She then chose to switch to the day’s math lesson, and we began the Bedtime Math warm-up (Monster Trucks). When we reached a problem requiring conversion of 66 inches into feet and inches, A’Lore disengaged and indicated she was finished; attempts to re-engage, including use of the merit system, were unsuccessful. This behavior was unexpected, as A’Lore’s regulation had improved after other scholars were pulled out. Notably, she completed her post-session student survey with all top scores. On reflection, I will review behavioral expectations at the start of future sessions and implement the tutor-versus-scholar competition to support focus and sustained engagement.

It's kind of hard to get a good gauge of how much they really understood because when I went over the basics of a clock with which hands tells what (EX: the short one is the hour hand the longer one is the minute hand, each number for minutes you count by 5s) it felt like they weren't getting it super well. But then when I had made an example on the demonstration clock they understood it and they could recreate times I asked them to make ont he demonstration clock so it seemed like they understood the basics of how to read a clock when its presented to them, but the finer points of what is a minute hand and what is an hour hand got lost in translation somehow. They enjoyed the body clock game but that didn't go as well as just the physical clock in their hand making the the time. So I think for the foreseeable future I will do a clock lesson once a week until they get the concept fully, and my other lesson will be more number and operation focused so they can keep practicing that, because I feel like a full 2 weeks dedicated to telling time might be counterproductive, but if I keep them on their toes and refresh it once a week it could better time spent on it because they understand the rudimentary nature of being able to say and read the clock and make it, but it was understanding and describing what the clock hands stand for which was where their issues lied. A lot of the issues come with not being able to add properly or understand why they are adding the way they are. An example was 6x6 used in class today. Math is often misunderstood as a dry collection of formulas, but at its heart, it is the ultimate logic puzzle. The true joy of learning math lies in the "aha!" moment—that instant when a complex problem suddenly snaps into focus, revealing a hidden pattern or a sleek solution.
It is a universal language that allows us to decode the world around us. From the symmetry of a snowflake to the algorithms that power our favorite apps, math provides a sense of wonder by showing us that the universe isn’t random; it’s structured and predictable. Mastering its rules feels like gaining a superpower, giving you the tools to build, calculate, and strategize with precision.
Moreover, math is a playground for creative thinking. While there is often one right answer, there are infinite ways to reach it. This freedom to experiment makes every problem an opportunity for discovery, transforming a classroom subject into a lifelong adventure in problem-solving.

sharon - Siena arrived engaged, confident, polite, and respectful. I believe she felt supported and comfortable during our session, and it seemed we began building a positive connection.

At this time, Siena isn’t yet writing independently — she copied from my model, and even with that support, she still had a few misspellings. That said, she stayed engaged and continued trying her best throughout. With consistent encouragement and scaffolding, I’m confident she’ll make steady progress.

I think she felt supported and comfortable, and it seemed like we began building a nice connection — though of course, it’s only the first day, so we’re still in the “honeymoon” phase.
